s843.content:
Eugene was a cleric of Toledo who slipped away to Zaragoza to live as a monk under St. Braulio, until the king called him back to be archbishop of Toledo in 647.

He was a poet and a lover of the Church’s music, and he improved the chant of his cathedral. He led the councils of Toledo and taught the young Julian, who would succeed him. He died in 657.
s843.intercession: St. Eugene, pray for us, and for all who sing the praises of God. Amen.

s844.content:
Anastasius was a monk, priest, and abbot of St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai in the seventh century. He traveled through Egypt and Syria defending the faith of Chalcedon, that Christ is one Person in two natures, divine and human.

His Hodegos, or Guide, was a handbook for those who had to answer the heretics, and he gathered many questions and answers on the spiritual life, and stories of the monks of Sinai, for the instruction of believers.
s844.intercession: St. Anastasius, pray for us, that we may know Christ truly God and truly man. Amen.

s845.content:
Eulogius was a monk of Antioch who became patriarch of Alexandria around 580 and governed that Church until his death in 608. He wrote against the many divisions of his day, defending the faith of the Council of Chalcedon.

He was a close friend of Pope St. Gregory the Great, and their letters survive; Gregory told him of the mission he had sent to the English and of the many baptized there.
s845.intercession: St. Eulogius, pray for us, and for the friendship of all who serve the Church. Amen.

s846.content:
Paulinus was a grammarian of northern Italy whom Charlemagne brought to his court, among the scholars of the Carolingian renewal. In 787 he was made patriarch of Aquileia.

He defended the faith against the error of Adoptionism, which said that Christ in his humanity was only an adopted son of God, and he sent missionaries to the Avars and the Slavs, insisting that they be taught before they were baptized, and never forced. He also wrote hymns, among them the Ubi caritas, sung on Holy Thursday.
s846.intercession: St. Paulinus, pray for us: where charity and love are, God is there. Amen.

s847.content:
Paschasius was a foundling raised by the nuns of Soissons who became a monk and then abbot of Corbie in northern France. Around 831 he wrote the first full treatise on the Eucharist, On the Body and Blood of the Lord, teaching that the body of Christ in the sacrament is the same body that was born of the Virgin and suffered on the cross.

He also wrote long commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and on the Lamentations, and lives of the abbots of Corbie. He resigned as abbot to return to study and prayer, and died around 865.
s847.intercession: St. Paschasius, pray for us, that we may adore the body and blood of Christ. Amen.

s848.content:
Simeon was bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the capital of the Persian Empire, and head of the Church of the East. When King Shapur II began a great persecution of the Christians, who he feared were friends of Rome, Simeon was ordered to collect a double tax from them and to worship the sun. He refused.

He was put to death on Good Friday, with about a hundred bishops, priests, and other Christians, who were killed before his eyes. It was the beginning of forty years of persecution in which countless Persian Christians died for Christ.
s848.intercession: St. Simeon, pray for us, and for all Christians who suffer in the Middle East. Amen.

s849.content:
Eustochium was the daughter of St. Paula, a noble Roman widow, and like her mother a disciple of St. Jerome, who wrote for her a famous letter on virginity. In 385 she went with her mother to the Holy Land, and they settled at Bethlehem near the cave of the Nativity.

There Paula founded monasteries, and Eustochium led the community of women after her mother died. She knew Greek and Hebrew, and helped Jerome with his translation of the Bible; several of his prefaces are addressed to her and her mother. She died at Bethlehem around 419.
s849.intercession: St. Eustochium, pray for us, that we may give our hearts wholly to Christ. Amen.

s850.content:
Blaesilla was the eldest daughter of St. Paula and sister of St. Eustochium. Widowed at eighteen, she enjoyed the life of a wealthy young woman of Rome, until a serious fever turned her heart, and she gave herself to prayer, fasting, and the study of Scripture under St. Jerome.

She died only a few months later, at twenty, worn by her penances. Her death caused anger in Rome against Jerome, and his letter consoling her mother is among his most tender.
s850.intercession: St. Blaesilla, pray for us, and for all young people who seek God. Amen.

s851.content:
Leontius was bishop of Fréjus in Provence in the early fifth century, and a friend and protector of the monks. He gave the island of Lérins to St. Honoratus for his monastery, which grew into one of the great centers of monastic life in the West.

St. John Cassian dedicated to him the first part of his Conferences, the conversations of the desert fathers that taught the West the monastic way.
s851.intercession: St. Leontius, pray for us, and for all who help others to pray. Amen.

s852.content:
Rabanus was a monk of Fulda who studied under Alcuin and became the greatest teacher of his age, called “the teacher of Germany.” As abbot of Fulda he made its school and library famous, and in 847 he became archbishop of Mainz, where he fed hundreds of the poor every day in a famine.

He wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible, an encyclopedia of all things, a book on the training of the clergy, and poems in praise of the cross. The hymn Veni, Creator Spiritus is traditionally said to be his.
s852.intercession: St. Rabanus, pray for us: come, Creator Spirit, and fill our hearts. Amen.

s853.content:
Simplician was a priest of Rome who instructed St. Ambrose in the faith when Ambrose was suddenly made bishop of Milan, and remained his spiritual father. St. Augustine went to him too, in the months before his conversion, and Simplician told him the story of the conversion of the philosopher Victorinus, which moved Augustine deeply.

When Ambrose died in 397, Simplician, by then an old man, succeeded him as bishop of Milan, and died around 401.
s853.intercession: St. Simplician, pray for us, and for all who guide others to the faith. Amen.

s854.content:
Severus was a wool weaver of Ravenna, a married man with a daughter. Tradition says that when the people gathered to choose a bishop, a dove came down and rested on him, and they chose him.

He was bishop of Ravenna in the fourth century, and attended the Council of Sardica in 343, where the bishops upheld St. Athanasius and the faith of Nicaea. He is the patron of weavers.
s854.intercession: St. Severus, pray for us, and for all who work with their hands. Amen.

s855.content:
Syncletica was the daughter of a wealthy family of Alexandria. When her parents died she gave away everything, cut her hair, and went with her blind sister to live in a tomb outside the city, where women gathered to learn from her. She is the most quoted of the desert mothers.

“In the beginning there are a great many battles and a good deal of suffering for those who are advancing toward God,” she taught, “and afterward, ineffable joy. It is like those who wish to light a fire: at first they are choked by the smoke and cry, and by this means they obtain what they seek.” She died at about eighty, after a long and painful illness borne with patience.
s855.intercession: St. Syncletica, pray for us, that we may persevere through the smoke until the fire is lit. Amen.

s856.content:
Poemen, whose name means “shepherd,” was a monk of Scetis in the Egyptian desert, and is the father most often quoted in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. He was known less for great fasts than for his gift of guiding souls, with gentleness and few words.

“Do not give your heart to that which does not satisfy your heart,” he said. And when brothers asked whether they should wake those who slept during the prayers, he answered, “For my part, when I see a brother dozing, I put his head on my knees and let him rest.” He taught that the nature of water is soft and stone is hard, yet the dripping of water wears away the stone: so the word of God, heard often, opens a hard heart.
s856.intercession: St. Poemen, pray for us, that we may be gentle with others and patient with ourselves. Amen.

s857.content:
Sisoes was a monk of Scetis who, after the death of St. Anthony, went to live in Anthony’s cave on the mountain by the Red Sea, and stayed there more than sixty years. He was known for his deep humility.

When he was dying, the brothers saw his face shine, and he spoke as if to people they could not see. He said he was asking for a little more time to repent. “You have no need to repent, Father,” they said. “Truly,” he answered, “I do not know if I have even begun.” Then his face shone like the sun, and he died.
s857.intercession: St. Sisoes, pray for us, that we may always be beginning to repent. Amen.

s858.content:
Pambo was a disciple of St. Anthony the Great who lived in the Nitrian desert, where many monks gathered around him. He was so careful with his tongue that he would often think for days, even years, before answering a question. St. Athanasius and St. Melania the Elder came to visit him.

When Melania brought him three hundred pounds of silver for the monks, he told a disciple to give it to the poorest monasteries without even looking at it. “Do you know how much it is?” she asked. “He to whom you have given it,” he said, “does not need you to tell him its weight.” At his death he said he could not remember a day he had eaten bread he had not earned, or said a word he had afterward regretted, and yet he went to God as one who had not yet begun to serve him.
s858.intercession: St. Pambo, pray for us, that we may guard our tongues and give in secret. Amen.

s859.content:
John, called Kolobos, “the short one,” was a monk of Scetis and a disciple of Abba Ammoes. The Sayings tell that his elder planted a dry stick in the sand and told him to water it every day; the water was so far away that he had to leave in the evening and return in the morning. After three years the stick put out leaves and bore fruit, and the elder took it to the church and said to the monks, “Come and taste the fruit of obedience.”

John was humble and easily forgot himself in prayer. He used to say that a house is not built from the top down, but from the foundation upward; and the foundation is our neighbor, whom we must win.
s859.intercession: St. John, pray for us, that we may bear the fruit of obedience. Amen.

s860.content:
Paphnutius was a disciple of St. Anthony who became bishop of a city in the Upper Thebaid in Egypt. In the persecution of Maximinus he was tortured for Christ: one of his eyes was put out and his leg was hamstrung, and he was sent to labor in the mines.

He came to the Council of Nicaea in 325 still bearing those wounds, and the Emperor Constantine is said to have kissed his empty eye socket. He remained a firm defender of St. Athanasius.
s860.intercession: St. Paphnutius, pray for us, and for all who bear wounds for Christ. Amen.

s861.content:
Thaïs, as the old story tells, was a courtesan of Alexandria, famous for her beauty, who had led many into sin. A desert monk came to her as if he were a client, and spoke to her of God and of judgment. She burned her fine clothes and jewels in the square and went with him to a convent in the desert, where she lived enclosed in a cell for three years, praying, “You who made me, have mercy on me.”

When she came out, she lived only fifteen days more among the sisters, and died in peace. Her story, told and retold for centuries, has always been read as a promise that no one is beyond the mercy of God.
s861.intercession: St. Thaïs, pray for us: you who made us, have mercy on us. Amen.

s862.content:
Theodora was a married woman of Alexandria who, according to her legend, fell into adultery and was overwhelmed with sorrow. To do penance she disguised herself as a man and lived among the monks of a monastery near the city under the name of Theodore.

Falsely accused of fathering a child, she said nothing in her own defense, and was driven out to live in the desert, where she raised the child herself for seven years. Only at her death was it discovered that she was a woman, and her innocence of the charge.
s862.intercession: St. Theodora, pray for us, that we may repent with our whole heart. Amen.

s863.content:
Chariton was a Christian of Iconium, in what is now Turkey, who was tortured for the faith in the last persecution and survived. On his way to Jerusalem as a pilgrim he was captured by robbers and held in a cave in the Judaean desert; tradition says that the robbers died by drinking poisoned wine, and Chariton turned their cave into a church.

He is honored as the founder of the first lavras of the Judaean desert, communities of hermits who lived in separate cells and gathered for prayer at the end of the week: at Pharan, near Jericho, and at Souka. He is said to have arranged the order of hours of prayer that the monks of Palestine followed.
s863.intercession: St. Chariton, pray for us, and for all who pray in the Holy Land. Amen.

s864.content:
Alypius was a deacon of Adrianopolis in Paphlagonia, in Asia Minor, who climbed a pillar near the city to pray, following the example of St. Simeon the Stylite. He lived on it, tradition says, for more than fifty years, exposed to wind and snow.

People came to him from every side for counsel and healing, and two monasteries grew up at the foot of his pillar, one of men and one of women, to which his mother and sister belonged. Mothers who long for children ask his prayers.
s864.intercession: St. Alypius, pray for us, and for all who long for children. Amen.

s865.content:
Theodore came to St. Pachomius as a boy of fourteen and became his most beloved disciple, so gifted that Pachomius sent him to teach the brothers while he was still young. Once, when Theodore was tempted to think he might succeed Pachomius, he confessed it, and Pachomius removed him from all office; Theodore accepted it in peace.

After Pachomius died, the great federation of monasteries he had founded fell into quarrels, and Theodore was called to lead it. By his humility and gentleness he held it together, until his death in 368. St. Athanasius wrote a letter of comfort to the monks when he died.
s865.intercession: St. Theodore, pray for us, that we may accept humiliation with peace. Amen.

s866.content:
Euphrasia was the daughter of a nobleman of Constantinople related to the Emperor Theodosius. After her father’s death her mother took her to Egypt, where she asked, at the age of seven, to stay in a monastery of nuns. When she was twelve, the emperor wanted to arrange a marriage for her; she wrote asking him to give her wealth to the poor and set her slaves free, and he did.

She lived the rest of her short life in the monastery, doing the humblest work, such as carrying stones, to fight temptation, and was loved for her charity. She died at thirty.
s866.intercession: St. Euphrasia, pray for us, and for all who give their youth to God. Amen.

s867.content:
Bessarion was a monk of Scetis, a disciple of St. Anthony and St. Macarius, who lived as a wanderer with no fixed cell, sleeping in the open and possessing only a cloak and a book of the Gospels. Many wonders were told of him: that he made salt water sweet for his thirsty disciple, and brought rain in a drought.

Once, when a brother who had sinned was sent out of the church, Bessarion rose and went out with him, saying, “I too am a sinner.” Another time he sold his book of the Gospels to give the money to a poor man, saying, “I have sold the very book that told me: Sell what you have and give to the poor.”
s867.intercession: St. Bessarion, pray for us, that we may stand beside every sinner. Amen.

s868.content:
John was a carpenter who, at twenty-five, became a monk and spent the last fifty years of his life walled up in a cell on a cliff near Lycopolis, today Asyut in Egypt. Through a small window he spoke to those who came to him on Saturdays and Sundays, and he was famous across the empire for his gift of prophecy and healing.

He foretold to the Emperor Theodosius his victories, and told him the time of his death. Pilgrims came from far away to see him, and he received them with joy, but he would not let women see him, sending blessings to them instead.
s868.intercession: St. John, pray for us, that we may listen to God in silence. Amen.

s869.content:
Amma Sarah was one of the desert mothers, who lived for sixty years by a river in the Egyptian desert, it was said, without once lifting her eyes to look at it. She struggled for thirteen years against a temptation of the flesh, and never prayed for it to be taken away; she prayed only, “O God, give me strength.”

When some monks came to humble her, saying that she was only a woman, she answered, “According to nature I am a woman, but not according to my thoughts.” And she said, “If I prayed God that all people should approve of my conduct, I should find myself a penitent at the door of each one. I shall rather pray that my heart may be pure toward all.”
s869.intercession: St. Sarah, pray for us, that our hearts may be pure toward all. Amen.

s870.content:
Marcella was a noble widow of Rome who, after only seven months of marriage, turned her palace on the Aventine Hill into a house of prayer and study, the first community of its kind among the women of Rome. St. Jerome taught there during his years in the city, and she questioned him so closely on the Scriptures that he called her the glory of the women of Rome.

When the Goths sacked Rome in 410, they broke into her house looking for treasure; she had given everything to the poor. They beat her, but spared the young woman with her. She died a few days later, at eighty-five.
s870.intercession: St. Marcella, pray for us, and for all who study the word of God. Amen.

s871.content:
Marcellina was the elder sister of St. Ambrose and St. Satyrus. In Rome, on Christmas Day around 353, she received the veil of a consecrated virgin from Pope Liberius, who preached a sermon on virginity that her brother later wrote down.

She lived a life of prayer and fasting in Rome, and then in Milan near her brother the bishop, who wrote his books On Virgins for her and asked her advice in the struggles of his Church. She outlived both her brothers, and is buried in the basilica of St. Ambrose.
s871.intercession: St. Marcellina, pray for us, and for all consecrated women. Amen.

s872.content:
Servatius was bishop of Tongeren, in what is now Belgium, in the fourth century, and the first known bishop in the Low Countries. He gave shelter to St. Athanasius in exile, and he defended the faith of Nicaea at the councils of his time.

According to Gregory of Tours, he foresaw the invasion of the Huns and went on pilgrimage to Rome to pray at the tombs of the apostles. He died at Maastricht, where his relics rest in the great basilica that bears his name, and he is one of the “ice saints” whose days in May come before the last frosts.
s872.intercession: St. Servatius, pray for us, and for the people of the Low Countries. Amen.

s873.content:
Dionysius was bishop of Milan from 349. At the Council of Milan in 355 the Arian emperor Constantius II demanded that the bishops condemn St. Athanasius. Dionysius first gave way, then, at the urging of St. Eusebius of Vercelli, withdrew his signature and refused.

He was sent into exile in Cappadocia, in Asia Minor, where he died around 360. St. Basil the Great later sent his relics home to Milan.
s873.intercession: St. Dionysius, pray for us, that when we fall we may rise again to the truth. Amen.

s874.content:
Benedict, born Witiza, was a Visigothic noble who served at the courts of Pepin and Charlemagne before becoming a monk. He tried at first to live by the severest rules of the East, then found in the Rule of St. Benedict the wise and moderate way he had been seeking, and founded a monastery on his own land at Aniane.

The Emperor Louis the Pious made him the guide of all the monasteries of his empire. At the councils of Aachen in 816 and 817 the Rule of Benedict was made the rule for every monastery, and he gathered the rules of East and West into a single book. He is called “the second Benedict.”
s874.intercession: St. Benedict, pray for us, that we may find the way of moderation and peace. Amen.

s875.content:
Robert was a monk of Champagne who in 1075 founded the abbey of Molesme for hermits who wanted to live by the Rule of St. Benedict in its first simplicity. When Molesme grew rich and comfortable, he left it in 1098 with about twenty monks for the marshy wilderness of Cîteaux, near Dijon.

There they founded the New Monastery, the beginning of the Cistercian Order. The next year the pope ordered Robert back to Molesme, and he obeyed and governed it until his death. He is honored with St. Alberic and St. Stephen Harding as the founders of the Cistercians.
s875.intercession: St. Robert, pray for us, that we may seek God in simplicity. Amen.

s876.content:
Alberic was a monk of Molesme who went with St. Robert to found Cîteaux in 1098, and became its second abbot when Robert was called back. In years of hunger and poverty he held the young community to its first purpose, and obtained the pope’s protection for it.

The Cistercians remember him as the one who gave them their white habit, and who placed the monastery under the protection of the Virgin Mary, to whom every Cistercian church is dedicated. He died in 1109, and St. Stephen Harding succeeded him.
s876.intercession: St. Alberic, pray for us, that we may be faithful when the way is hard. Amen.

s877.content:
Majolus was the fourth abbot of Cluny, and governed it for forty years. He reformed monasteries across France, Burgundy, and Italy at the request of kings and emperors, and was so trusted that the Emperor Otto II wanted him to be pope; he refused.

In 972, crossing the Alps, he was captured by Saracen raiders, and the monks of Cluny paid a great ransom to free him. His abbey gave Europe a model of prayer, of the liturgy sung with beauty, and of freedom from the power of local lords.
s877.intercession: St. Majolus, pray for us, and for all who renew the life of the Church. Amen.

s878.content:
Berno was a monk who reformed the abbey of Baume in Burgundy. In 909 or 910, Duke William of Aquitaine gave him land at Cluny to found a new monastery, placed directly under the protection of the pope and free from the control of any lord or bishop.

Berno was its first abbot. From this small beginning came the great reform of Cluny, which spread to hundreds of monasteries and renewed the Church of the Middle Ages.
s878.intercession: St. Berno, pray for us, that what we begin for God may bear fruit. Amen.

s879.content:
Æthelwold was a monk of Glastonbury under St. Dunstan who restored the ruined abbey of Abingdon, and in 963 was made bishop of Winchester. With St. Dunstan and St. Oswald he led the great revival of monastic life in England after the Viking raids, replacing worldly clergy with monks and refounding abbeys across the land.

He drew up the Regularis Concordia, a common rule for all the monasteries of England, and translated the Rule of St. Benedict into English. A great teacher, his school at Winchester trained a generation of scholars. He was called “the father of monks.”
s879.intercession: St. Æthelwold, pray for us, and for all who rebuild what has been lost. Amen.

s880.content:
Oswald was of Danish family, raised by his uncle St. Oda, archbishop of Canterbury, who sent him to be a monk at Fleury in France. He became bishop of Worcester in 961 and archbishop of York in 972, and with St. Dunstan and St. Æthelwold he renewed the monasteries of England, founding Ramsey Abbey among others.

Every day he washed the feet of twelve poor men. He died in Lent in 992, at Worcester, just after washing their feet, kneeling as he said the Gloria Patri.
s880.intercession: St. Oswald, pray for us, that we may serve the poor as Christ did. Amen.

s881.content:
Ceolfrith was abbot of the twin monastery of Wearmouth and Jarrow in Northumbria, and the teacher of St. Bede, who came to him as a boy of seven. Bede tells that when plague emptied the monastery, only the abbot and one boy were left to sing the whole office; that boy was probably Bede himself.

Ceolfrith had three great Bibles copied. In 716 he set out for Rome, old and ill, to bring one of them as a gift to the pope, and died on the way at Langres in France. That Bible, the Codex Amiatinus, still survives in Florence, the oldest complete Latin Bible in the world.
s881.intercession: St. Ceolfrith, pray for us, and for all who teach the young. Amen.

s882.content:
Cedd was a monk of Lindisfarne, trained by St. Aidan, and the brother of St. Chad. He brought the Gospel to the Middle Angles and to the East Saxons, became their bishop, and built churches, among them the chapel of St. Peter-on-the-Wall at Bradwell, which still stands.

He founded the monastery of Lastingham, and at the Synod of Whitby in 664 he served as interpreter between the Irish and the Roman sides. He died of plague at Lastingham soon afterward.
s882.intercession: St. Cedd, pray for us, and for all who carry the Gospel to new lands. Amen.
